title: One hundred studies, two passes
hook: What does a 36% significant-replication rate actually count?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Distinguish a significant replication count from a claim that the remaining effects are all exactly zero.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Distinguish a significant replication count from a claim that the remaining effects are all exactly zero.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: An illustrative set has 36 significant reruns out of 100. What share is not significant? Toy inputs A=[36, 100]; B=[60, 100].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[36, 64, 64], [60, 40, 40]]. Labels: Significant %, Not significant %, Not significant n.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: A replication-significance count is not a count of effects proved exactly zero. The two case totals show how the fraction is formed. Interpreting any non-significant result also requires its precision, design and target effect.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Significant reruns=60, Total reruns=100. What is Not significant %? Answer: 40.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Significant reruns=60, Total reruns=100. What is Not significant %?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 40. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.section: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceProvenance.text: Only about 36% of 100 published psychology findings replicated with significant results (Open Science Collaboration, 2015).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Distinguish a significant replication count from a claim that the remaining effects are all exactly zero.
